thesis: Calista publishes a roster of Shareholders it can't reach, and none of what it costs is published anywhere.
brief:
Calista maintains a page called the Shareholder Address Unknown List. It was updated on July 1, 2026, and the page describes the people on it as "Shareholders unable to receive distribution checks, voting materials or newsletters by mail." No count is printed on it. We counted the entries on the page and got 127. That is our count of your page, not a figure you published, and you can repeat it.

On another page Calista tells Shareholders what the mail channel costs them. A distribution sent by direct deposit arrives the same day. Sent by mail it takes three weeks or longer in rural Alaska. Those are Calista's own descriptions, quoted in full later in this study.

We spent this study on that gap. What we would build is a work queue for Shareholder Services that gathers every piece of evidence about one unreachable name onto a single screen, proposes candidate matches using rules a person can read line by line, and then refuses to change anything until a named person confirms it. Confirmed Shareholders, and a cohort you choose from those still on mail, get a one-tap invite to direct deposit and electronic delivery that opens on a phone and works with no signal.

Phase one contains no model at all. The one place a model would genuinely help, reading scanned paper, does not appear until a second phase and ships only if it passes a test agreed beforehand. If that test set does not exist, it does not ship and the rules stand alone.

The honest cost picture is a range with one end that says no. Our conservative case recovers about 32 percent of five-year cost and never pays back. Our middle case pays back around month 44, which is slow for a build this size and we are not going to dress it up. That figure also assumes a quarter of invited Shareholders accept, a rate nobody has measured, and at a tenth it does not pay back at all. What separates them is how large an invitation programme you decide to run and what a mailed item really costs you, and neither is published. That is exactly why we are proposing a two-week look at your records for six to eight thousand, and then a ten-week pilot at $40,500 if it survives that, plus about a thousand dollars of print and postage and your own staff's time on the follow-ups, which sit outside that number and are described below.

What we could not verify matters as much. Calista publishes no case volume, no backlog, no cycle time, and no split between Shareholders paid by mail and by direct deposit. Producing eight such numbers is the first deliverable. Seven land by week eight and the eighth, the acceptance rate, lands at week twenty, and together they are what should decide whether anyone spends more, including on us.

What we are asking for is an hour, not a decision.

found.title: Calista already publishes the problem, and keeps it current
found.lede: The strongest evidence in this study is a page Calista maintains itself.
found.body:
Most companies make you go looking for the operational gap. Calista posts it. The Shareholder Address Unknown List carries the names of owners of the corporation who can't receive their distribution checks, their voting materials, or their newsletter, and it was refreshed on July 1, 2026. That it is public and current is a governance choice we would defend, not a criticism.

What the page does not carry is a number. We counted the entries and got 127. We are telling you how we got it because you can open the page and count it yourself.

Against a base Andrew Guy described to the Senate Committee on Indian Affairs as "more than 39,500 Alaska Native Shareholders, with approximately 20,000 living throughout our ancestral Homelands in the Yukon-Kuskokwim Region," 127 is a small share. It is also the share where the corporation's basic obligation to its owners is not being met.
found.callout_note: Names on the July 1, 2026 roster. Our count of the page, which publishes no total of its own.
found.body_2: The distributions work next door to this is visibly manual, and Calista describes it that way itself. Calista's live posting for a Shareholder Distributions Coordinator asks that person to "Research and calculate payments owed to deceased Shareholders and identify those that must be voided or stopped then redistributed to rightful heirs," and notes that "Although the standard work week is scheduled at 40 hours, overtime hours may be required to meet objectives and project deadlines."

costing.title: The cost is a three-week wait, and the rest is not published anywhere
costing.lede: We can describe the shape of what this costs. We can't honestly size it, and neither can anyone else from outside.
costing.body: Calista's own distributions page states the cost, and it is written for Shareholders rather than for a proposal. Direct deposit arrives "The same day as the distribution, but verify with your individual bank." Mail takes "3 weeks or longer, especially in rural Alaska, from the day of distribution." For a Shareholder on the roster there is no arrival date at all, and the ballot and the newsletter do not arrive either.
costing.callout_note: The gap between the two ways Calista pays a distribution, in Calista's own description of them.
costing.body_2: We looked for eight numbers and found none of them published: how many Shareholders can't be reached, how much mail comes back each distribution cycle, the split between mail, direct deposit and electronic delivery, how long a returned mailing waits before anyone works it, how many reconnections are confirmed rather than merely matched, how many staff minutes a confirmation and an enrollment follow-up each take, what a printed and mailed item actually costs you, and what share of invited Shareholders accept. Producing those eight is the first deliverable of the pilot, seven by week eight and the acceptance rate at week twenty, and it is why the pilot is worth buying on its own.

opportunity.title: What changes is that a name stops waiting for a relative to notice it
opportunity.lede: Walk one returned envelope through the process as it runs today, and then as it would run.
opportunity.outcome_body: The outcome we would aim at is narrow on purpose. Reconnect the Shareholders Calista can't currently reach, and move more Shareholders onto same-day direct deposit and electronic delivery, so fewer owners wait three weeks or longer for money that is already theirs.

before_after.headline: One returned distribution check, today and after

rows.today: A distribution check comes back undelivered. The envelope joins a stack on a desk.
rows.after: The returned mailing enters a work queue the moment it is logged, with the Shareholder's record already attached.

rows.today: Someone searches several systems by hand, and a spelling that does not match exactly returns nothing.
rows.after: Candidate records are proposed and ranked, including spellings and village names that do not match exactly.

rows.today: The name is published on the roster and waits for a relative to see it, and nothing records who looked or what they found.
rows.after: The name is still published, and every step now carries a name, the evidence that was seen, and a timestamp.

rows.today: A person decides whether this is really the same Shareholder.
rows.after: A person decides whether this is really the same Shareholder.

rows.today: A reconnected Shareholder stays on paper, and the next distribution takes three weeks or longer.
rows.after: A reconnected Shareholder gets a one-tap invite that works with no signal, and the next distribution can arrive the same day.

before_after.note: The Today column is our reconstruction from what is public, not something we watched, and replacing it with what actually happens in your office is the first thing the two-week look buys. The fifth row is deliberately identical. Deciding that two records are the same person is the one step we would not automate at any confidence level, because a wrong match removes the name from the roster while the Shareholder still receives nothing, and the only person who would notice is the one you already can't reach.

opportunity.after_body: A match score is stored against a candidate and never against a Shareholder record, and the software that proposes matches has no permission to record a confirmation at all. A record moves only when a person acts on evidence they can see.

build.title: Most of what we would build is not AI
build.lede: A work queue, matching rules a person can read, an evidence panel, an audit trail, and an enrollment invite that survives a satellite connection.
build.plain_parts: A list of the people you can't reach. A table of name and village spellings your own staff write. A matcher that proposes who each person might be. A screen showing the evidence. A confirm button only a person can press. An invite that opens on a phone with no signal. A record of who decided what, and when.
build.what_it_does: The queue takes the roster and returned mail as its work list. The matcher compares each unreachable name against your records using rules a person can read, chiefly a table of Yukon-Kuskokwim name and village spellings your own staff write and Calista owns outright. Every candidate lands in a state called matched but unconfirmed and stays there. A person in Shareholder Services opens the evidence, confirms or rejects with a reason, and only then does a record change. The enrollment invite then goes to two groups, the Shareholders you reconnect and a cohort you choose from those currently receiving by mail. The AIRRAQ network covers 13 Western Alaska communities, seven more villages are due by the end of 2027, and most of the rest run on satellite, so an invite that needs a live connection is an invite much of the region can't accept, which is why it stores answers on the phone and sends them when signal returns.
build.feasibility:
Phase one contains no model at all. Chain four judgments together, each right nine times in ten, and the arithmetic lands at about two thirds right end to end, which across a roster this size is dozens of wrong records, wrong silently. With no model in the path, reliability is something you verify by testing rather than estimate.

One place a model would genuinely earn its keep is reading scanned and handwritten records that rules can't read. That is phase two, and it is gated. If roughly 100 past resolutions do not exist in a form we can test against, or the step does not clear an accuracy bar written down before we run it, it does not ship and the rules stand alone.

You already answered the hardest question here yourselves, when you posted a Shareholder Services receptionist where "Ability to speak Yupik strongly preferred." We would not sell anything that quietly displaces that person, and we would not build anything that translates Yugtun. Two separate things support that, and they are worth keeping apart. A California contractor, Accent on Languages, produced Yup'ik disaster materials that KYUK translator Julia Jimmie described by saying "They were Yup'ik words all right, but they were all jumbled together, and they didn't make sense." That was human work. Separately, reporting on machine translation of these languages describes a poor record, "often providing inaccurate sentences and even completely invented words." In a region where nearly half the population, some 10,000 people, learn Yugtun before English, neither of those is a risk worth taking with your own language.
build.build_vs_buy:
We would buy the hosting, the sign-in, the postal address lookup and the message delivery, all inside your own cloud account. We would build the queue, because the case-management tools we have used resolve a record once a score crosses a threshold, and the first thing we would do is check whether yours can be made to refuse. That behaviour is what would drop a Shareholder off the roster while she still receives nothing.

You could also build much of this yourselves. Calista has a Chief Information Officer, and a Full Stack Developer role open in Huntsville. If your answer on the call is that your own team should build the rest, that is a good outcome and we would scope it that way.

architecture.caption: Read left to right. Calista's records and a variant table your staff write go in. The match finder proposes candidates and decides nothing. Everything waits in the queue until a person in Shareholder Services confirms it against the evidence. Only then does a record change, signed with who did it. Nothing on this page uses a model.

roi.title: The conservative case does not pay back, and that is the argument for a small pilot
roi.lede: Three scenarios, one of which says no. What separates them is how many Shareholders you are willing to invite and what your own mail actually costs, and neither of those is published.
roi.lede_body: Every figure below is computed from the drivers printed with it. Two things to be plain about before you read it. The top row counts Shareholders who accept and move off mail, which is an outcome rather than a number anyone controls, and the cohort you would have to invite to get there is printed lower in the table as invitations a year needed at a quarter accepting, and whether a quarter of them actually accept is the thing the pilot tests. That same quarter is assumed in all three columns, so the range below does not bracket that risk. At a tenth accepting the middle case never pays back either. Rolling that invitation out across the Shareholder base is real work that is not in the ten-week price. Its print and postage is now inside the five-year cost below. The staff time to run it is not, and neither is the follow-up each acceptance creates. No row is marked verified, because Calista publishes no internal volumes, so there is nothing here we could check against your own numbers.
roi.table_caption: Five-year total cost of ownership against modelled benefit. Computed, not narrated.

roi.table_note: How to reproduce every figure. Mail handling avoided is the standing cohort times touches times cost per item times the share that disappears, and the standing cohort is the yearly acceptances accumulated over the horizon. Reconnection carrying cost applies that same share to $60, $75 and $90 a year per unresolved record, covering returned postage, void and reissue banking fees and the unclaimed-property administration on a record nobody can deliver to, and it contains no staff time. Reissue cost applies that share to 1.5, 2.0 and 2.5 percent of the checks that would otherwise have been mailed to that cohort, at $55, $65 and $75 an event. The Shareholders you reconnect also join the electronic cohort, so a small part of those last two lines overlaps. On the same average-standing basis the rest of the table uses, that is roughly two to three percent of the annual benefit depending on the column, and we have not netted it out. The reconnection line also assumes the queue extends past the published roster to all returned mail, which is a Next-lane item and not in the ten-week price. The 127 names on the roster alone support roughly three and a half years at the conservative rate and under two at the aggressive one, and how much returned mail arrives after that is one of the numbers the pilot measures. Five-year benefit runs the first year at 30, 40 and 50 percent of run rate for a mid-year go-live, then four full years, so it is 4.3, 4.4 and 4.5 times the annual figure rather than five. Cost of ownership is the two-week look plus the $40,500 pilot, plus run cost of $12,000, $9,000 and $6,500 a year for 4.5 years, plus contingency of 20, 18 and 15 percent. The look is quoted at six to eight thousand and the model uses the top of that range. The invitation programme is now costed rather than assumed away, and its volume scales with the column, because an invitation is itself a printed and mailed item. At the gate's rate of a quarter accepting, 700 acceptances needs 2,800 invitations a year, 1,600 needs 6,400, and 3,000 needs 12,000. The Aggressive column therefore requires more than four times the volume the gate paragraph describes, and 3,000 acceptances could not come from 2,800 invitations at all. Against the more than 39,500 Shareholders quoted earlier, that column means inviting close to a third of everyone you have, every year for five years. It is printed as a ceiling. We would not plan on it and we did not use it for the payback figure. Those invitation costs sit in run cost above. What is still NOT costed anywhere is the staff time to run that programme, and it is large enough to move the answer. At the middle column's 1,600 acceptances a year, even ten minutes of follow-up each is roughly 270 hours, about seven weeks of one person's time, against a $42,593 annual benefit, and it would move it against us. The pilot's own 500 invitations, roughly $600 to $1,050 of print and postage, sit outside the $40,500 as well. Assumptions we chose, rather than facts about Calista: the acceptance count, the touches, the two distributions a year, the item cost, the share that disappears, the reconnection rate, the $60 to $90 a year carrying cost per unresolved record, the 1.5 to 2.5 percent reissue rate, the $55 to $75 per reissue event, and the quarter of invitations that accept. That is the complete list of numbers we picked. The last one is the sharpest. At a tenth accepting rather than a quarter the conservative column needs 7,000 invitations a year and the middle column needs 16,000, and on those numbers the middle case recovers 78 percent of its cost and never pays back either. Note what 16,000 means. It is more than the 12,000 the Aggressive column needs, which is already close to a third of every Shareholder you have, so at a tenth accepting the middle case is not merely slower, it needs a mailing programme larger than the ceiling we just said we would not plan on. The pilot's acceptance leg exists to test that rate before anyone spends against it. No hours-times-rate line appears anywhere.
roi.payback_range: Share of five-year cost recovered in the conservative case, which does not pay back inside the horizon. On those assumptions the $10,500 a year of benefit does not cover the $15,360 a year it costs to run once the invitations are counted, so it loses money every year rather than merely paying back slowly. Most likely pays back at month 44, on the same assumption that a quarter of those invited accept.
roi.base_rate_note: The outside view cuts against us, and it is why this build is deliberately dull. S&P Global Market Intelligence surveyed more than 1,000 respondents in North America and Europe and found the share of companies abandoning most of their AI initiatives jumped to 42 percent from 17 percent the year before, with the average organization scrapping 46 percent of its proofs of concept before they reached production. That direction is worse year over year. In your own contracting world, Deltek, which sells software to government contractors, surveyed 917 of them and found 45 percent unclear on the return from AI. That is a vendor's own study and we are handing it to you as one, which is the same test we are about to apply to the peer figures. The peer figures we found were vendor-authored with no baseline published, so they tell you nothing about what Calista would get.
roi.value_owner: Shareholder Services owns the number, with the Chief Information Officer owning records access and the cloud account it runs in, and the Chief Financial Officer countersigning the measured baseline at the end of the pilot so the gate number is finance's number and not the project's.

roadmap.title: A two-week look, then ten weeks of work against a stop rule that closes at week twenty
roadmap.lede: The conservative column is the floor below which we tell you to stop, and the middle column is the shape of worth building. That column pays back at month 44, which is slow. Most software of this cost is judged against twelve to twenty-four months, and a payback past two years is normally a reason to ask whether this is the right solution at all. It is exactly why the decision belongs at week twenty on measured numbers rather than on this model, because even the model's good case is slow.
roadmap.body: The first two weeks are the look, and your own staff work your own records on your own machines while we observe and time it, so nothing leaves the building. In the pilot that follows, everything we touch before records clearance runs on the public roster and synthetic records, so one record is carried the whole way before any real record moves to us.

now.item: A two-week look at your own records, in your office, on your machines, with nothing leaving the building. Forty names from the roster worked by your staff while we time it, against a rule written down before we start
now.metric: If fewer than 16 of the 40 have any internal evidence to work with, we say so in writing and the pilot does not proceed

now.item: Records access and legal clearance, started day one with a named owner on both sides, because it is the longest pole and it is not ours to pull
now.metric: Signed terms by the end of week three, with data staying in your own cloud account and Calista owning every derived artifact including the variant table

now.item: One record carried the whole way, from the roster through matching to a person's confirmation to an enrollment invite
now.metric: One record completes the path with an unbroken audit trail before any piece is deepened

now.item: The measurement layer, producing the eight numbers that are not published today
now.metric: Seven of the eight produced by week eight. The acceptance rate reads at week twenty, because invitations and their replies each cross rural mail

now.item: Invite a pilot cohort of 500 Shareholders from the mail list, chosen by you, and sent under your name after you sign off the wording
now.metric: Acceptances per hundred invited, released in week three and read at week twenty, reported separately for the communities with fiber and everywhere still on satellite. The week-ten count is a floor, not the rate

now.item: A name and place variant table built with your staff, in your database, yours outright
now.metric: The share of queue records where at least one variant-table rule fires, taken in week three as the baseline and again in week ten. We are not setting a target now, because there is no prior number to set it against

next.item: Extend from the published roster to all returned mail, timed to your distribution and annual meeting cycles
next.metric: Confirmed reconnections as a share of the roster counted at the start, cycle over cycle

next.item: The one model-assisted step, reading scanned records, which ships only if it earns its place
next.metric: Measured against cases already resolved, against a bar agreed before the test. If roughly 100 past resolutions can't be found in a testable form, it is not built and the money is not spent

next.item: Estate and heirship evidence assembly, every line linked to its source image, never determining an heir
next.metric: How many heirs a closed case eventually found are surfaced by the packet

later.item: Benefits ledger reconciliation across the subsidiaries, with zero AI, because exact matching on structured records is right every time and your own people can do it
later.metric: Unexplained differences at each month close. May never be collected, and nothing here depends on it

later.item: Land and material sale intake, which is a web form with a routing rule
later.metric: Share of enquiries arriving complete enough to route without a follow-up

later.item: Take the enrollment invite to the whole Shareholder base rather than a pilot cohort. This is where most of the avoided mail handling in the table actually comes from, and it is not in the ten-week price
later.metric: Shareholders moved off mail per distribution cycle, against the split the pilot measures in week eight

roadmap.gates: Four gates, and you can stop at any one and keep everything produced to that point. They are the two-week look, records clearance, the ten-week stop rule, and phase two. Clearance opens before any real record moves, and if it never opens the pilot ends at the measurement layer, no further money is asked for, and you keep the baseline, the queue design and the variant table. The phase-two gate is the only one whose most likely answer is no. The stop rule is the conservative column above, stated numerically in advance so nobody can move it later, and it is the FAIL LINE rather than the build line. The two record-side legs read at week ten, at least 7 confirmed reconnections and a measured cost per mailed item of at least $1.20. Hitting those exactly is not a reason to build, because the conservative column loses money every year. They are the floor below which we stop, you pay nothing further, and you keep the baseline, the queue design and the variant table. To be worth building the numbers have to come in above the floor, and the middle column is the shape of above, about 11 confirmed reconnections in the ten weeks rather than 7, and a measured cost per mailed item nearer $1.60 than $1.20. Even that column pays back only at month 44. For payback to land inside two years your measured mail cost would have to run well above $1.60, or the invitation programme would have to be materially larger than 6,400 a year. Of those two we think the mail cost is the likelier, because it is the one number you can pull off an invoice rather than a number you have to go and create. The acceptance leg does not separate the floor from above, because the same quarter accepting is assumed in all three columns, so 125 of 500 is the reading either way. The acceptance leg can't be read then and we are not going to pretend it can. Invitations release in week three and your own page puts rural mail at three weeks or longer each way, so the count at week ten is a floor and not the rate. The acceptance leg reads at week twenty, at least 125 acceptances from the cohort of 500. The middle number is a quarter of those invited, and the arithmetic connecting it to the 700 a year in the conservative column is that 700 acceptances at that rate needs roughly 2,800 invitations a year, which is the rollout in the Later lane and is not in the ten-week price. All three are among the eight numbers the pilot produces, so nothing in the gate rests on a figure you take on faith. The record side closes at week ten and the acceptance leg closes at week twenty, and week twenty is the date the decision to spend more should be taken. Nothing is billed between those two dates. We send you the count and that is the last thing the pilot owes you.
roadmap.need_from_you: A named owner in Shareholder Services. Counsel's sign-off on records access started in week one rather than week five. Two to three hours from the CIO's team up front. About three hours a week of Shareholder Services time, which is a real cost to a small team and the dependency we would most want you to push back on now. Separately, and outside those hours and outside the $40,500, an accepted invitation starts a request that one of your people finishes through the process you already run. At 125 acceptances that is 125 follow-ups, and we would rather you saw that number now than met it in week twelve. We also need a yes or no by week two on whether roughly 100 past resolutions exist, because that answer decides whether phase two contains a model at all.

honest.title: The evidence to reconnect these people may not be in your records
honest.lede: Three things, and we would rather raise them than have you find them.
honest.body:
The riskiest assumption is that evidence to reconnect these Shareholders already exists inside Calista's own records. If it does not, the matcher has nothing to work with and the right answer is an outreach campaign, not a work queue. We would retire that first, with the two-week look described above, six to eight thousand dollars, run in your office on your machines with no data leaving the building. Take forty names from the roster, have your own staff work them while we time it, and write the decision rule down beforehand. If fewer than 16 of the 40 have any internal evidence, we say so in writing and the pilot does not proceed.

The second is that our headline metric could lie to us. A shrinking roster looks like success even when a record was matched to the wrong person, so confirmed reconnections are counted separately, every resolution is audited rather than sampled, and the reconnection line in the business case counts only confirmed reconnections, never matches.

The third is that you may build this yourselves, and we have said so above rather than hoping it does not come up. The pilot is shaped so everything of lasting value belongs to you whether we build phase two or not. Landing exactly on the conservative column is not a reason to build either, because that column loses money every year. It is the floor below which we stop.

next_step_title: The next step is a conversation, not a signature
next_step: If this is useful, the most valuable hour would be spent on a question we could not answer from outside. We have no visibility into how your federal proposal operation actually runs, and it may well be the largest opportunity of this kind anywhere in the company. We did not rule it out. We ruled out recommending something we can't see.
